doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Life experience and the blues in great players
summary: Life experiences shape the playing; Nussbaum hears the blues in Trane, Armstrong, Holiday and Hendrix.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: That’s right. And to have that kind of thing where you make people get some kind of feeling. That’s something. And as you grow up in this world, as you start to deal with life and the things that you have to deal with as far as realities of life, you know, wife, kids, family, being out here in the world working with everybody, you know all these things effect you. You know everything that happens to you effects you. You know people you © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

love, people that come and go, people that die, whatever. All these things effect you. And they all help to shape you and when you play this is all part of your life experience. And this is all part of what’s out there on the line. And when you’re playing you’ve got to be thankful for that experience. You’ve got to get out there and play your ass off. You could be dead tomorrow. You can’t feel like you’re jiving anybody. You’re on the line. It’s for real. And when you’re in a great band it’s a great feeling because if everybody’s got that kind of feeling going on it’s a great thing. It’s an indescribable thing. You know there are those moments in your life where you feel like the music is playing you. You’re just like a vehicle for stuff that comes out when you’re in that other space. And those are the things that keep you going.

But it’s definitely not a technical thing. I mean you have to have enough technique to convey, to be able to manifest this thing that’s happening, but technique is — nothing against technique — but it has to be up to a certain level but it’s definitely not a technical thing.

I mean you hear Trane, I’m aware of the feeling. I’m not aware of the amazing chops that he had to do it. It’s like you hear a man really playing from his soul. I mean to me, it’s like any of the great players I hear, whatever technical brilliance they have, you never lose the blues. The blues is always somehow there in any of the people that you dig. I mean you heard it all the time with Louis Armstrong. You hear it with Billie Holiday. You hear it with Trane. You hear it with Sonny. You hear it with somebody that makes you feel something. And that’s the thing that I, I mean it’s not even just jazz it’s all the other music too. Jimi Hendrix, with all the stuff he did pushing the envelope with the guitar. Man, underneath it that was some serious blues going down. When I hear Rubenstein playing Chopin nocturnes, you’re getting it. I mean you feel it. And that’s, for me that’s all the stuff that’s effected me. It’s like how does it make you feel? It’s not like did you see that? Well no, it’s like wow—
And how did you like it. It’s not like how are you doing, it’s like how are you feeling?
